Translate the smallest enclosing-circle center to zero. By the supplied optimality fact and Carathéodory's theorem, there are $m\leq3$ contact points $x_i$ and positive weights $\lambda_i$ with $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$ and $\sum_i\lambda_ix_i=0$. Each contact has $|x_i|=R$, so expanding squares gives
$$\sum_{i,j}\lambda_i\lambda_j|x_i-x_j|^2
=2\sum_i\lambda_i|x_i|^2-2\left|\sum_i\lambda_ix_i\right|^2=2R^2.$$
The diagonal summands vanish; every other distance is at most $w$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\sum_i\lambda_i^2\geq1/m\geq1/3$, hence
$$2R^2\leq w^2\left(1-\sum_i\lambda_i^2\right)\leq\frac{2w^2}{3}.$$
This proves $R\leq w/\sqrt3$.

Equality forces $m=3$, all weights $1/3$, and every mutual contact distance equal to $w$: the contacts form an equilateral triangle. Conversely, an equilateral triangle of side $w$ requires enclosing radius $w/\sqrt3$, so any diameter-$w$ set containing one attains equality. If the set is also a constant-width body $K$, its diameter bound puts it in the three radius-$w$ disks centered at these contacts. Their intersection is the width-$w$ Reuleaux triangle $T$. Inclusion $K\subset T$ between equal-width bodies forces equality: $h_T-h_K\geq0$ and its antipodal sum is zero. Thus the constant-width equality case is exactly the Reuleaux triangle.

The dilation $E\mapsto aE$ bijects the admissible competitors for $\Omega$ and $a\Omega$. Planar finite-perimeter scaling gives $P(aE)=aP(E)$ and $|aE|=a^2|E|$; taking infima proves $h_C(a\Omega)=h_C(\Omega)/a$. If $\Omega\subset\Lambda$, every competitor in $\Omega$ is admissible in $\Lambda$, proving $h_C(\Omega)\geq h_C(\Lambda)$.

For $E\subset B_R\subset\mathbb R^2$, the isoperimetric inequality gives
$$\frac{P(E)}{|E|}\geq\frac{2\sqrt\pi}{\sqrt{|E|}}\geq\frac2R.$$
The choice $E=B_R$ attains the bound, so $h_C(B_R)=2/R$. Here perimeter means the full Euclidean perimeter, not relative perimeter measured only inside $\Omega$; the latter convention would give a different problem.

solutions.body_md:
The erosions $K_{-t}$ decrease with $t$. Their areas are continuous on $[0,r]$. One way to see the only nontrivial interior step is to choose an incenter $c$: for $0\leq t<t+\varepsilon\leq r$,
$$c+\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{r-t}\right)(K_{-t}-c)\subset K_{-(t+\varepsilon)}\subset K_{-t}.$$
Indeed every support inequality for $K_{-t}$ has an available margin at least $r-t$ at $c$. The inclusions squeeze the areas, and also give left continuity by starting at $t-\varepsilon$. At $r$, continuity from above follows from continuity of measure for the decreasing compact erosions. The terminal set $K_{-r}$ has zero area: if a convex set of centers had interior, it would contain some ball $B(c,\varepsilon)$, forcing $B(c,r+\varepsilon)\subset K$ and contradicting the inradius.

Thus $F_K(t)=A(K_{-t})-\pi t^2$ is continuous and strictly decreasing on $[0,r]$: its first term is nonincreasing, while $-\pi t^2$ is strictly decreasing for $t\geq0$. Moreover $F_K(0)=A(K)>0$ and $F_K(r)=-\pi r^2<0$. The intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity give exactly one root $t_K\in(0,r)$.

For comparing bodies, set eroded area equal to zero after an erosion becomes empty. If $A(K_{-t})\geq A(L_{-t})$ for $0\leq t\leq t_L$, then at $t_L$ the right side is $\pi t_L^2>0$, so $t_L<r(K)$. Therefore $F_K(t_L)\geq0$ implies $t_K\geq t_L$ and, by the supplied Cheeger characterization, $h_C(K)\leq h_C(L)$. The geometric comparison determines the ordering; the characterization itself is a theorem assumed in the question.

The sets intersect precisely when $b-a\in K-K=wB$. For interiors, use the convex-body identity $\operatorname{int}(K-K)=\operatorname{int}K-\operatorname{int}K$. One quick justification is that the right side is open and convex, and its closure is $K-K$ (approximate each boundary point from the interior); an open convex set is the interior of its closure. Thus interior intersection occurs exactly for $|a-b|<w$.

At equality the intersection is nonempty but has empty interior. A separating hyperplane between the two interiors supports both bodies at any point of contact. Constant-width bodies are strictly convex, so that hyperplane meets each body in only one point. Consequently the contact is unique. For larger displacement even the closed bodies do not meet.

If $N\geq2$, the common point is on the boundary of every body: an interior neighborhood in one body would intersect interior points of any other body arbitrarily near $p$. Each tangent cone at $p$ is a closed sector of angle $\alpha_i\in[2\pi/3,\pi]$ by the corner bound; a smooth point has angle $\pi$.

The interiors of these angular sectors are disjoint. To see this, a ray direction in the interior of a convex body's tangent sector enters its interior for all sufficiently small positive distances from $p$. This follows by choosing two nearby directions realized by points of the body on opposite sides of the ray and taking their convex hull with $p$. A direction interior to two sectors would therefore produce an interior overlap near $p$.

Hence $\sum_i\alpha_i\leq2\pi$, and $N\leq3$. If $N=3$, all three angles equal $2\pi/3$ and no angular gap remains. The equality case of the corner theorem makes each body a Reuleaux triangle with vertex $p$. Their widths may differ; the angular conclusion does not require equal size.

solutions.body_md:
Every admissible body contains $0$ by the enclosing-ball core lemma. The common-point packing theorem gives at most three; in an arrangement of three, each is a Reuleaux triangle with its $120^\circ$ vertex at $0$, and the three tangent sectors partition the full angle.

For existence, take a centered equilateral triangle with vertices $v_1,v_2,v_3$ and side one, and let $T=\bigcap_iB(v_i,1)$ be its Reuleaux triangle. Use the three translates $T-v_i$. Each contains $0$ and lies in $B(0,1)$ because $T$ has diameter one. Their tangent sectors at $0$ have angle $120^\circ$ and equally spaced bisectors directed along $-v_i$; they therefore have disjoint interiors. Equivalently, the translation differences all have length one. Each pair meets only at $0$.

The equality case already fixes a Reuleaux triangle from its vertex and its two extreme tangent rays. Thus, up to a common rotation or reflection and relabeling, this is the only three-body arrangement.

Its occupied area is $3(\pi-\sqrt3)/2$, a fraction $3(\pi-\sqrt3)/(2\pi)\approx0.673007$ of the disk. An arrangement of at most two bodies has total area at most $2(\pi/4)=\pi/2$, which is smaller. Thus the same three triangles maximize total occupied area. Finally, if boundary contact is forbidden, at most one body is possible because every pair contains $0$; a single radius-$1/2$ disk shows this bound is attained.

The three-body classification in the disk proves that three congruent copies can fit only when $K$ is a Reuleaux triangle. The construction in the preceding exercise proves sufficiency, even using translations only.

Here is an independent translation formulation. The condition $K+t\subset B(0,w)$ says $-t\in E_w(K)=K$, so $t\in-K$. Pairwise nonoverlap says $|t_i-t_j|\geq w$. Since $-K$ has diameter $w$, all such distances must equal $w$. A planar equidistant set has at most three points: after placing two points, the two possible third points are at distance $\sqrt3w$ from each other and cannot both be used. If three exist, their negatives form an equilateral triangle inside $K$. The diameter-$w$ bound puts $K$ inside the Reuleaux triangle determined by those vertices. Inclusion of two bodies of the same constant width forces equality, because their nonnegative support difference has zero antipodal sum. Thus again $K$ must be the Reuleaux triangle. If one center is zero, another gives $2a\leq R-a$, which is already stronger than required. Otherwise arrange the four directions cyclically. One angular gap is at most $\pi/2$. For the corresponding pair, $c_i\cdot c_j\geq0$, whence
$$4a^2\leq|c_i-c_j|^2\leq|c_i|^2+|c_j|^2\leq2(R-a)^2.$$
Thus $R\geq(1+\sqrt2)a\approx1.020367$.

For the upper bound, use four radius-$1/2$ disks with centers $(\pm1/2,\pm1/2)$. Neighboring disks touch, and all four fit in the radius-$\sqrt2/2+1/2$ disk. Consequently $R_4\leq1.207107\ldots$. The argument neither determines $R_4$ nor asserts that the optimizing shapes are disks.

solutions.body_md:
By the translation collision criterion, admissibility is exactly $|v|\geq w$ for every nonzero $v\in\Lambda$. Choose a shortest nonzero vector $a$. It is primitive (otherwise it is an integer multiple of a shorter lattice vector), so it extends to a lattice basis $(a,b)$; in integer coordinates this is the elementary Bézout property for a coprime pair. Replace $b$ by $b-ma$ so its component $t$ parallel to $a$ has $|t|\leq|a|/2$. Since $a$ is shortest, $|b|\geq|a|$, and the perpendicular component satisfies $|b_\perp|\geq\sqrt3|a|/2$. Therefore the fundamental-cell area is
$$D=|\det(a,b)|\geq\frac{\sqrt3}{2}|a|^2\geq\frac{\sqrt3}{2}w^2.$$
The triangular lattice generated by $(w,0)$ and $(w/2,\sqrt3w/2)$ attains this: the squared length of an integer combination is $w^2(m^2+mn+n^2)\geq w^2$ unless $m=n=0$.

The packing density is $A(K)/D$, proving the formula. For the disk it is $\pi/(2\sqrt3)\approx0.906900$; for the Reuleaux triangle it is $\pi/\sqrt3-1\approx0.813799$. The fixed-width maximum-area inequality shows that the disk uniquely maximizes this density among constant-width bodies. This conclusion concerns lattice packings of translates and does not optimize packings in which different copies can rotate independently.

solutions.body_md: For any integer $m\geq6$, let $u_j=(\cos(2\pi j/m),\sin(2\pi j/m))$ and take the $m$ triangles $\operatorname{conv}\{0,u_j,u_{j+1}\}$ (indices modulo $m$). They lie in the unit disk and in sectors with disjoint interiors. Each has two sides of length one and a third side $2\sin(\pi/m)\leq1$, so its diameter is exactly one. Each has positive area. Taking $m$ arbitrarily large, or choosing any desired number of triangles from a larger arrangement, proves the assertion. Their widths are not constant: in narrow directions they are much smaller than one. In particular their corner angles at the center can be arbitrarily small, so the $120^\circ$ constant-width argument does not apply.
